description: We're a US-based team that wants to build something NASA mission planners would actually use, not just a pretty demo. Our focus: the Moon and Mars, especially the challenge Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars. We're interested in how open NASA data from Earth, the Moon and Mars can help choose where to test equipment before it flies.
summary: Mission Alive is an interactive web academy for ages 10-14, built for the challenge 'Abandoned but not Forgotten.' Six real NASA machines that never came home — the Apollo 17 lunar rover, Surveyor 3, Curiosity, Ingenuity, the Webb telescope, and Voyager 1 — call the player for help. In six playable missions the player repairs a broken fender, lands a probe, codes a rover's drive, flies a helicopter in thin Martian air, unfolds a golden mirror, and sends a greeting across interstellar space, earning six stamps toward a crew certificate. Each machine speaks in its own voice and hands the player one thing to carry home: resourcefulness, evidence, patience, daring, precision, endurance. The app runs on real NASA data: Voyager 1's live distance from JPL Horizons, live Deep Space Network contacts, and Ingenuity's full 72-flight log — and Voyager crosses one light-day on November 18, while judges are reading this. details:
What it does and how it works

Mission Alive is a free web app for ages 10 to 14. No install, no account, no microphone. The player is a new cadet answering calls from six real NASA machines that never came home: the Apollo 17 lunar rover, Surveyor 3, Curiosity, Ingenuity, the Webb telescope, and Voyager 1. Each mission is a different playable job. The player builds and dust-tests a replacement fender for the rover, probes the soil and picks a landing patch for Surveyor 3, programs Curiosity's drive with command blocks, steers Ingenuity to a landing zone, unfolds Webb's mirror wings and aligns three star images to reveal infrared light, and answers Voyager 1 by writing a greeting to send across interstellar space. Every mission ends with a stamp and a final transmission in the machine's own words. Six stamps open a graduation finale and a printable certificate. A full run takes about 13 minutes. Progress is saved on the device, and the app works with keyboard, pointer, or touch, with a 2D view for devices without WebGL and a Reduce Motion setting.

Benefits

For players, the app lets them do the job instead of reading about it, and each machine hands them one thing to carry home: resourcefulness, evidence, patience, daring, precision, endurance. For teachers, a built-in For Teachers page offers a classroom guide, session modes, a standards map, and printable activity packs. For anyone, the app runs in a browser, costs nothing, and needs no account. A Playtest impact page inside the app shows live results from player feedback, updated from the response sheet.

Intended impact

Kids love space but rarely see themselves in it. In a 2019 LEGO and Harris Poll survey of 3,000 children aged 8 to 12, 86 percent were interested in space exploration, but only 11 percent wanted to be an astronaut, against 29 percent who wanted to be a YouTuber, and science interest fades from ages 10 to 11 and drops sharply at 14. Mission Alive is built for exactly that age window: it puts the player inside the job, not in front of a poster. In a playtest with 13 players, all friends aged 18 to 22 rather than the 10 to 14 target audience, feeling that space was "for people like me" rose from 1.54 to 3.54 out of 5, interest in space rose from 2.15 to 3.77, and 69 percent finished all six missions. These are voluntary, self-reported results, so they are early signal, not proof.

Tools and technology

Built with JavaScript, HTML, and CSS on Vite, with Three.js for the 3D machine scenes and a 2D fallback where WebGL is unavailable. Hosted on Netlify, with Netlify functions caching live data from JPL Horizons and the Deep Space Network. The source is public on GitHub. Machine narration voices were generated with ElevenLabs. Live data includes Voyager 1's distance from JPL Horizons, live Deep Space Network contacts, Ingenuity's complete 72-flight log, and 55 Golden Record greetings. The project passed 111 automated tests covering certification, localization, data freshness, accessibility, and all six missions. AI use is disclosed on the project page: Codex assisted with code and ElevenLabs supplied the narration voices.

How it is creative

The machines are the narrators, not the subject. Each one speaks in the first person, asks for help with its own real problem, and hands the player a named virtue at the end. Six different game genres sit inside one passport: build, probe, code, fly, align, listen. The story spine is the six things the player carries home, not a score. And the live Voyager counter turns a real spacecraft into a character the player can watch: Voyager 1 crosses one light-day on November 18, 2026, during judging week.

What the team considered

Accuracy first: every exhibit was checked against NASA sources, and simulations are labeled as teaching models, separate from NASA measurements. The Voyager counter is labeled an estimate from JPL Horizons, not a live signal from the spacecraft.

Age: short text, one goal per mission, big targets, and a visible passport so a 10-year-old always knows what to do next.

Access: English, Spanish, and Vietnamese interfaces, Reduce Motion, sound-off completion, written alternatives to audio, and no account.

Privacy: no analytics, progress stays on the device, and greetings stay private unless the player chooses to share.

Honesty about AI: where AI was used is disclosed, and AI did not generate the idea.
